operations.name: Fred Suttle

expected.name: Fred Suttle
expected.description: Fred Suttle was given a five- to ten-year prison sentence for violating the state's criminal syndicalism law because he belonged to the IWW. While in prison Suttle suffered a mental breakdown and was transferred from Walla Walla Prison to the state hospital for the insane. He was released after nearly seven years in prison on September 24, 1928.

operations.source: Aaron D. Jesch, The Industrial Workers of the World and the Performance of Protest, discussion explicitly identifies Fred Suttle, WSP 9176, born Missouri August 1884, citing his prison biographical statement: https://www.ibew.org.uk/dvarch/DV04833.pdf . Same text indexed in Washington State University thesis repository. MONTH precision; day unknown. Historical state register is explicitly prefixed WSP, not a federal BOP number.

operations.name: Sigfrid Stenberg

expected.charges: Federal prosecution under the Espionage Act of 1917 and/or the Sedition Act of 1918 (mass IWW trial in Chicago).
expected.sentence: ADMITTED TO BAIL, APRIL 2, 1919. The Federal Circuit Court of Appeals ordered thirty-eight of the men convicted in the Chicago mass trial released on bail pending its review of the case; the bonds ran from $5,000 to $10,000, with Haywood alone required to provide $15,000. Fifty-five others convicted in the same case did not seek bail. The order is not the release: each man left Leavenworth when his bond was actually furnished, which for those whose dates are recorded here fell between April 28 and September 28, 1919. Reported in the New York Times and across the wire services, April 3, 1919.

updates.convicted: Yes — convicted at the mass IWW trial in Chicago

operations.source: Stephen M. Kohn, American Political Prisoners (1994): https://dokumen.pub/american-political-prisoners-prosecutions-under-the-espionage-and-sedition-acts-0275944158-9780275944155.html . Individual Stenberg entry, page 134. Source distinguishes September 1917-November 1919 and April 1921-November 1922 custody. No single continuous counter created from separated episodes; populated bail-order narrative preserved.
